#742. Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon

It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.

That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.

In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.

Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.

On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.

One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.

French giants Lyon outclass Arsenal in Women's Champions League

Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.

In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.

Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.

Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.

Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.

"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.

"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."

Despite playing at right-back, Jule Brand had the third most touches in the Arsenal penalty area for Lyon (five) after striker Marie-Antoinette Katoto and fellow goalscorer Melchie Dumornay

Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.

Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.

Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.

As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.

Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.

Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.

"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.

"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."

Arsenal have not yet qualified for the knockout stages of the Champions League

Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.

They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.

"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.

"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."

It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.

Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.

They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.

Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.

Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.

Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.

"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.

"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.

"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."

#741. The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

"Sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.)

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#739. Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United head coach will be at Liverpool on 22 November

"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

Matheus Cunha's injury-time goal against Roma on 3 November sealed one of only three Manchester United victories in 15 games this season

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

Diogo Dalot is consoled by Manchester United team-mate Joshua Zirkzee after being substituted during the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Liverpool and Man Utd fans give predictions ahead of Premier League match

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

Why does Pochettino keep lemons in his office?

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a Â£50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with Â£70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

Further forward, with Benjamin Sesko out, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo have tended to be used in the number nine role. But Cunha likes to drop deep, while, after a bright start to the season, Mbeumo has scored twice in his past 12 appearances.

Neither Shea Lacey nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Both caught the eye on England Under-20 duty during the international break. Pochettino has history for giving young players a chance and the pair could benefit from that.

Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe have been the subject of numerous supporter protests and chants

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than Â£1.1bn and a further Â£14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

#738. Bruno Mars Announces Death of Dad in Heartbreaking Post

Bruno Mars shared that his dad Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74, writing in an emotional tribute, "In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world."

Bruno Mars knows his dad was amazing, just the way he was.

The “That’s What I Like” shared that his father Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74 and shared a heartfelt tribute to the impact he had on his life.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time,” Mars wrote on Instagram Nov. 19. “If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music.”

The 41-year-old—whose real name is also Peter Hernandez—added that his father helped raise six children, including Mars, his sisters Tiara, Tahiti, Presley and Jaime and his brother Eric, saying, “In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again.”

Mars—whose mother Bernadette San Pedro Bayot died from a brain aneurysm in 2013 at the age of 55—concluded his message by writing, “I Love you Pops. Kiss mom up there for me.”

Alongside the emotional message, the “Just the Way You Are” singer shared a photo of himself and his father sharing an embrace in a hospital bed along with several pictures of his father from throughout the years. He did not confirm his father’s cause of death.

Mars and his dad had shared a truly special bond through the years as the “Uptown Funk” singer’s love of music was inspired by his father’s own history of performing. While Hernandez was born in Brooklyn, he later moved to Hawaii, where he founded a doo-wop revival group called The Love Notes.

And from a young age, Hernandez—who split from Mars’ mother when the Grammy winner was 12—knew that his son was destined for greatness.

“He was a ham,” Hernandez told MidWeek about Mars in 2014. “As soon as he could walk and express himself, he had to be in the middle of everything and wanted to be a part of whoever he’d seen on TV.”

Of course, he was incredibly proud that his son was “the product of a lot of love from all his family.”

“No woman could ever love Bruno as much as his late mother did,” he added, “and no man could ever love Bruno as much as I love him.”

And Hernandez was there for his son right until the end, offering Mars advice on what to say when he was honored with a Las Vegas street named after him in April.

“He says, ‘My loving son, I know you don't like advice, but getting a street named after you is a monumental moment,’” Mars recounted in a video from the event shared by AP News. “‘I just wanna say, I know you must be very proud, ‘cause I’m so proud for you. If you are gonna say anything on the mic to the crowd, both God and people love humility. So be humble and tell your fans it's their street, and you're so honored and grateful.’”

#736. You Actor Alexander Haskin Dies at Santa Monica Pier

Alexander Haskin, a personal trainer who became a background actor after leaving the Air Force, died Nov. 15 at the age of 38 after entering the ocean near the Santa Monica Pier, according to police.

Police are investigating the tragic death of Alexander Haskin.

The 38-year-old—who appeared as a background actor on shows like You and The Rookie—was pronounced dead Nov. 15 shortly after he was pulled from the ocean outside the Santa Monica Pier in Los Angeles, the Santa Monica Police Department confirmed to The Los Angeles Times.

Police said they received a report at 4:06 p.m. Nov. 15 that a man was in the water. Harbor guards responded and removed Haskin from the ocean, hoisting him onto the pier deck, where the Santa Monica Fire Department paramedics continued lifesaving measures, police spokesperson Lt. Lewis Gilmour told the Times.

Despite their efforts, Haskin was pronounced dead shortly before 5 p.m.

The actor’s cause of death was deferred, pending further investigation, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office records obtained by the Times.

Meanwhile, Gilmour confirmed an investigation into Haskin’s death is underway, though he said a preliminary investigation found no suspicious circumstances.

Plus, police confirmed that Haskin had been alone in the moments before entering the water, despite reports that he had been in an altercation with another person.

“The evidence shows the man was alone and did not interact with anyone in the period immediately before the incident,” Gilmour told the Times. “Security footage corroborates that finding.”

Following Haskin’s death, his dad Dana Haskin told the Times that his son had seemed in good spirits when they last spoke on Nov. 13. He also shared that Haskin had sent him a short text the morning of his death, though he did not disclose the message’s contents.

He also remembered his son—an Air Force veteran and personal trainer—as a “multifaceted guy” who loved music, fitness and acting.

“He was a happy guy,” Dana Haskin told the Times. “He liked to joke around, and he was always getting in trouble, but in a good way.”

#735. The Deals: Yamaha Acquires Visual Technology Company Disguise for $280 Million & More

Also: Ovation Rights buys the copyrights to Jeff Wayne's Musical Version of The War of the Worlds, among other recent deals.

Yamaha Corporation, the musical instruments and audio products company, acquired Disguise, which provides visual technology for live events, location-based experiences and virtual production spanning software, hardware and creative and technical services. A public notice published by Yamaha on Friday (Nov. 13) pegs the price of the transaction at 215 million pounds ($281 million).

According to a press release, Disguise technology has powered the visuals for tours by Beyoncé, Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny, along with locations including the Burj Khalifa in Dubai and the Stade de France in Paris.

“Welcoming Disguise marks a major step for Yamaha as we move beyond the traditional boundaries of musical instruments and audio equipment to create new experiential value centred on sound and music,” Atsugi Yamaha, president/representative executive officer of Yamaha Corporation, said in a statement. “As part of our long-term growth strategy, we are expanding our audio business into adjacent areas, including entertainment. We will combine the strengths of Disguise and Yamaha while respecting the brand, technology, and global relationships Disguise has built with customers and partners. Together, we will make new waves in live entertainment.”

Following the acquisition, the Disguise “brand, identity and relationships with customers and partners will be preserved,” according to a press release, with Disguise becoming “a new pillar alongside Yamaha’s existing business.” — Chris Eggertsen

Entertainment rights company Ovation Rights acquired the underlying copyrights in Jeff Wayne’s Musical Version of The War of the Worlds and struck a long-term creative partnership with Wayne, who composed and produced the music for the best-selling 1978 double concept album that spawned a multimedia franchise, including an immersive experience. The deal will see Ovation Rights working closely with Wayne and his family to create new opportunities for the property across live entertainment, music and digital formats ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2028. There are also plans to relaunch the immersive experience.

According to a press release, Jeff Wayne’s Musical Version of The War of the Worlds has sold more than 16 million records worldwide since its 1978 release. It adds that over nearly 50 years, the album “has evolved into a global entertainment property spanning spectacular arena tours and is a Guinness World Record ™ title holder as the world’s longest-running musical immersive theatre production.” — Chris Eggertsen

Schubert Music Group acquired the group of indie publishing and recorded music catalogs of French music publisher Cyril Dohar, which were built over three decades. The group consists of Éditer à Paris, Grounded Music, Modjo Music and Editions Cyril Dohar, which collectively include song copyrights and master rights to works by global stars David Bowie, Fergie, Goldfrapp, Joe Strummer, Jarvis Cocker and Florence + the Machine, along with a French roster of works by Orange Blossom, Dope Saint Jude, Sandra Nkaké and Disiz. The repertoire additionally includes works by reggae star Pablo Moses, world music acts Groundation, Yotam Silberstein, Sam Mangwana and Touré Kunda, and the Beautiful Songs catalog. — Chris Eggertsen

Nonprofit record label family Smithsonian Folkways Recordings acquired two record labels: Voyager Recordings, which released fiddle music and other traditional music of the Pacific Northwest and elsewhere; and Bay Records, which focused on Northern California old-time, traditional folk, bluegrass, fiddle and string band music. Selections from both labels’ catalogs are now available to download or stream.

“Smithsonian Folkways is honored to bring Voyager and Bay Records back into circulation as part of our collection,” said Maureen Loughran, director/curator of Smithsonian Folkways, in a statement. “These labels both have important roles in documenting the folk music history and traditions of the West Coast, a history that is often overshadowed by the long- storied folk revival of the East Coast. What is found here are vibrant music traditions, fierce fiddle tunes, old folk songs, and a story of two labels with deep connections to the labels already within the Smithsonian Folkways Recordings collection.”

A full discography for Bay Records is available here and for Voyager Recordings here. — Chris Eggertsen

AYO Music Group, an invitation-only music copyright administrator, announced investments from Wu-Tang Clan founder RZA, Atlanta music executives and Disturbing The Peace Records founders Chaka Zulu and Jeff Dixon, family office CIH Group and New York entrepreneur David Goldberg. Founded by Deborah Mannis-Gardner, Pär Almqvist and Stacey Haber, AYO offers global administration of publishing, neighboring rights and recordings. Its clients include MC Lyte, Pete Rock, LeToya Luckett and Lil Mama. — Chris Eggertsen

Rendezvous Sound, a new electronic music label and publishing venture, officially launched. The company’s label component will operate as a joint venture with broke Records, with longtime industry exec Alexander Bonavia leading the company from London. Bonavia takes on the position after previous roles at  Hipgnosis, Warner Music Group and Wavo. After operating for less than a year, the company reports that it’s averaging 100 million streams a month.

“We are agile, aggressive and modern,” Bonavia says in a statement. “We bet that the left of center electronic artists selling out venues would start to cross over to streaming, and that bet has already paid off with such artists as Kolter, Beave, Adriatique, Beltran, Ben Sterling, Ayybo and Joshwa.”

“Alex is a sharp dealmaker, consistently able to find and close the records and artists who succeed in both club culture and streaming,” added broke CEO Andre Benz. “His international marketing experience has also been invaluable to our wider team.” — Katie Bain

Dubai-based independent music and entertainment company Afterpeak, founded by Avery Chauhan, signed an exclusive multi-year global distribution deal with Too Lost for both catalog and future releases. Too Lost has additionally provided Afterpeak with “multi-seven-figure financing” to support the company’s catalog growth, artist development, new music releases and international expansion.

According to the release, Afterpeak has more than 25,000 releases and over 3 billion Spotify streams under its belt since its founding 2020. The company describes itself as being focused on “a high-volume, internet-native approach to recorded music, combining creative development with technology, data and catalog management,” adding that it “has built thousands of recordings of popular works with producers and studio musicians around the world while increasingly expanding its focus on original music, artist development and licensing.” — Chris Eggertsen

Warner Music France invested in Délicieuse Musique, the indie company that operates a portfolio of labels including Délicieuse Records, Nice Guys, Noire & Blanche, Egoplanet, Crosswalk and Hip Dozer. Through the deal, Délicieuse labels will enjoy access to Warner Music Group’s global distribution, marketing, synch licensing and brand partnerships resources, in addition to the creative and studio resources of Warner Music France.

Délicieuse will continue operating independently, led by co-founders Mathieu Léglise and Gautier de Bosredon, with the company’s existing team continuing to operate out of its headquarters in Bordeaux, France.

Founded in 2012, Délicieuse encompasses 10 specialized imprints and manages a multi-genre roster of more than 1,200 artists. — Chris Eggertsen

Generative AI audio company Sonilo, which is building video-native music and sound models, struck a licensing deal with Symphonic. Under the agreement, Sonilo will license opted-in recordings from Symphonic to train its AI music model. A press release says Sonilo “will provide attribution reporting to support transparency and compensation for the rights holders behind the music.” — Chris Eggertsen

Lyrics provider Musixmatch and DistroKid renewed their global partnership via a new multi-year agreement. The DIY distributor will continue offering Musixmatch’s lyric distribution via its Lyric Blaster service, which allows artists to deliver their lyrics to major streaming and social platforms.

Musixmatch also announced a new partnership with music royalty collection and distribution platform Notes.fm. The deal will allow Notes.fm to bring synchronized lyrics capabilities to its distribution offerings. — Chris Eggertsen

Believe‘s b:electronic and new electronic music label STILL BE AROUND signed a partnership that will see both labels align on A&R scouting, playlisting, DJ promotion, performance marketing and more. Led by Andreas Weitkämper, STILL BE AROUND operates out of Hamburg, Germany, and Lisbon, Portugal. It has upcoming releases from artists including Roger Sanchez, KI/KI, Interplanetary Criminal and Jaden Bojsen. — Chris Eggertsen

Symphonic signed a deal with Roblox that will bring hundreds of thousands of curated Symphonic-distributed songs to the gaming platform for use in games and virtual spaces. Symphonic songs are now available in the Roblox Creator Store; the deal also covers use of the music in Roblox’s new Moments section, where players can watch gameplay captures from the Roblox community and discover new games to play. — Chris Eggertsen

Universal Music Canada (UMC) signed an A&R and label distribution partnership with First Class Music Group, launched earlier this year by Leo Strang and Jake Pretorious — 24-year-olds who co-founded the Toronto underground rap festival First Class Fest. The two companies will jointly sign and develop Canadian artists under the deal. The partnership also covers distribution. First Class Fest will remain separate from the UMC agreement. — Chris Eggertsen

#734. Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026

The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #733. Traitors: New Blood Crowns Winner After Tearful Final Moments

Traitors: New Blood revealed which contestant walked away with the prize pot during the Alan Cumming-hosted reality show’s two-part finale, which aired Nov. 19 on NBC.

Content warning: This story contains spoilers for the finale of The Traitors: New Blood.

One by one, the Faithful fell—and a new Traitors winner was crowned.

Ironworker Shane Beatty hammered out his spot in TV history when he became the sole winner of The Traitors: New Blood, the fifth season of the U.S. series, during the emotional two-part finale on Nov. 19.

Beatty, 32, made history as the first recruited Traitor to win the U.S. series. He joined Katie Fites in the turret after she recruited him in the Nov. 12 episode, following two consecutive Traitor banishments.

Thursday night’s two-part finale began with the banishment of Jay Vinnedge and the murder of Clyde Moser—two Faithfuls who had begun voicing suspicions about Beatty and Fites.

After the remaining contestants completed their final mission, the two Traitors survived the castle’s final Round Table, which ended with Kriste Lewis’ banishment.

Five contestants remained for the final banishment ceremony, but they all chose to continue banishing. Fites was sent out of the game, visibly shocked when Beatty turned against her. In the final vote, Victor Vollbrechthausen was banished, despite Beatty’s attempt to keep him in the game until the end.

With only three contestants left, Beatty revealed to Faithfuls Wyatt Gillespie and Abbey Benjamin that he was a Traitor before breaking down in tears.

“I’m sorry,” Beatty said, his face in his hands. “I’m so sorry, guys.”

Beatty explained that he had started the game as a Faithful but was given an ultimatum to either become a Traitor or be murdered. Despite their visible devastation, Gillespie and Benjamin embraced Beatty.

“You don’t got to explain it, bro,” Gillespie said. “I would’ve done the same.”

With the $246,300 prize pot before him, Beatty told host Alan Cumming that the winnings were life-changing.

“I can finally just feel like I’m not drowning under the water,” Beatty said. “I just feel like I’m barely making it, and I can change my life now.”

The Traitors: New Blood premiered in September as the first all-civilian season of the U.S. series.

The next season of The Traitors will premiere Jan. 14, 2027 on Peacock and will return to an all-celebrity cast, including Olympian Chloe Kim, The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’s Bronwyn Newport and The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Whitney Leavitt.

Read on for more secrets of the Traitors castle...

1. While scheming is certainly a hallmark of The Traitors gameplay, contestants have no choice when it comes to their Traitors vs. Faithful status. Though, starting with season two, stars like Phaedra Parks and Kate Chastain were able to plead their case to host Alan Cumming.

"That has a really big bearing on it, as does Alan’s opinion,” executive producer Mike Cotton noted to Variety. "It’s almost like a job interview to be a Traitor, and we take all of that into account and decide just before the pick who that should be. We want to make sure we’ve got an interesting mix of characters that will bring their own unique skill set to it."

Though it’s not immediately clear to the cast just how many among them are Traitors. "We knew that there could potentially be three to five Traitors in the game,” Survivor’s Cirie Fields told E! News in 2023 after her season one victory. "That was explained to us from the very beginning."

2. They were also instructed to commit to the Traitors oath: "Do you commit to lie and deceive throughout the game? Are you willing to murder your fellow players every single night? And, do you vow to keep your identity and the identity of your fellow players a secret?"

3. To help producers determine who might be best at backstabbing and bluffing, contestants take a personality test. "We see attributes that might make someone a good liar or particularly deceptive,” Cotton Variety. Still, "We actually don’t know who the Traitors are until that pick, where Alan walks around and taps them on the shoulder.”

4. As for Cumming, he was excited to sign on for his campy role and bring his little dog, too. Recounting the initial pitch to Daily Beast in 2023, "I said, 'It’s sort of like you want me to be like a Bond villain. And I should actually bring my dog and pet her.’ And they went, 'That’s a good idea' And I thought, oh, I want to do this.”

With rescue pup Lala on hand, he leaned hard into his role, quoting playwright William Shakespeare and philosopher Plato on-camera. "So I had this flaring-nostril sort of persona,” he told the outlet. "And you’re kind of making stuff up as you go along. Literally, sometimes, they’re feeding me lines in my ear. So it was a bit like doing stand-up comedy actually, because you’re just winging it."

5. The cast might have a royally good time in Scotland’s Ardross Castle, but they don’t actually get their own palace digs.

"None of us stayed in the castle,” Cumming divulged to the Daily Beast. Instead, he continued, "You come to Scotland, and you stay in the Inverness airport hotel." While he had his own nearby digs, "I had a room in the castle where I would get made up and dressed," he added. "It had a huge bed in it. So I did actually sleep quite often, but not overnight."

6. In fact, the cast almost navigated rougher seas. "My first idea was to do it on a ship in Australia, and if somebody had to be out of the game, he or she had to jump into the water and swim to an island," creator Marc Pos revealed to Variety, "but then I thought it would be too difficult to produce."

7. Contestants weren’t able to wade into every corner of the castle. "We use a section of it," Cotton explained to Variety. "We’ve taken a wing of the castle, and that’s their area that they can play the game within. They’ve got all the outside as well. They’re free to roam around."

But with enough square footage for some 30 bedrooms, he noted, "If we covered that huge space, it’d be impossible to cover them all. They can split up and have their own conversations, but it’s small enough that someone could be listening on the door outside, and someone can see when someone disappears and has their own secret chat."

8. Perhaps that’s why Big Brother alum Rachel Reilly shared that car rides to and from the challenges were the most ideal times to scheme with fellow players. "You’re separated, and nobody can hear what you’re saying," she explained to Reality Blurred. "In the castle, you have to whisper."

9. Game planning at the hotel, however, was strictly verboten. "You’re not supposed to talk about the game when the mics aren’t ready or the cameras aren’t on," season two player Dan Gheesling told Business Insider, "because if we say something that’s important and it’s not on camera, they can’t use it on the show."

10. Also not allowed, season three’s Chrishell Stause revealed, was a hair and makeup team. "I would’ve died to have glam in the castle,” she told Us Weekly, "but Alan [did] not allow us to."

11. In order to arrange the nightly murders, "It’s a massive military operation each night to get the Faithful to bed in individual rooms," Cotton told Variety, "and get the Traitors back out to have their meeting."

Even season two then-couple Larsa Pippen and Marcus Jordan weren’t able to share a room. "I think they would have wanted to," acknowledged executive producer Sam Rees-Jones, "but they weren’t allowed to because it would have given them a foot up in the game."

12. Still, Shahs of Sunset’s Reza Farahan attempted to get crafty. "I did try to sneak out of my room to leave notes… I was trying to have fun in the moments where you weren't supposed to have fun," he told Digital Spy. "I would leave notes under people’s doors that said, 'I know what you did last summer, signed The Traitors.'"

13. Not that there is all that much time for fun and games. "We mainly like to film an episode a day, which is quite a big undertaking," Rees-Jones detailed to Variety. "But the reason we like to do that is because it keeps an immersive bubble, keeps their heads in the game. Schedule-wise, it’s a real pressure, but content-wise, it’s definitely the right thing to do. We start the day with breakfast, have a roundtable, have a mission, have a murder and then start again." (Stause revealed there was one night they got back to their rooms at 2 a.m.)

While the breakfasts are a strategic operation where players are brought in at staggered intervals, Cotton told Variety, the meals last "from start to finish, an hour max."

14. Perhaps that’s why producers take strides to keep contestants sharp. "You can only drink one drink a night," Love Island winner Ekin-Su Culculoglu, a season two Faithful, told Entertainment Weekly in 2024, "it was quite restricted."

15. Though it can be hard to find true allies in-game, each player is assigned a welfare team member. "They’re checking on you at all times,” season two standout Mercedes Javid said on the Just Sayin’ podcast. "They’re so cheerful and professional. I felt taken care of at all times."

16. As for forming onscreen bonds, contestants don’t know who they’ll be competing alongside until they arrive in Scotland. "You don’t want them to be able to research each other," casting director Deena Katz explained to Time, "or talk to each other or form alliances before." But once the game kicks off, players receive cheat sheets on each other and a journal to take notes.

17. For the record, Cumming fancies himself a Traitor. "I think it’d be great to decide who to murder," he told the Daily Beast in 2023. "The thing about this game—people would sort of turn on people and say, 'Well, they did this and therefore that means they’re a Traitor.' Well, they’re a Traitor because I patted them on the shoulder. And that’s the only reason they’re a Traitor."

#732. University students are biggest spreaders of COVID

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a big part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

The study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest among adolescents aged 15 to 18 in schools, undergraduates at university, and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

The analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences with medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” says Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts, between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage says. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.

#731. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.

Astronauts' photos of innocuous space debris helped fuel belief in the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

#728. Darren Hayes Launches the 2026 ARIA Awards With Savage Garden’s ‘Affirmation’: Watch

The stirring performance was the starting point for the 40th annual ceremony.

Savage Garden is, sadly, long gone. But when Darren Hayes took the stage at the 2026 ARIA Awards on Wednesday night (Nov. 18) in Sydney, he reminded everyone tuned in exactly what they were missing. Explore Darren Hayes Savage Garden See latest videos, charts and news

Hayes got the 40th anniversary ARIAs broadcast underway — and the emotions stirring — with a performance of “Affirmation,” the title track from Savage Garden’s second and final album from 1999. Related Doja Cat Blasts Rockstar Games for Leaving Her Music Out of 'GTA 6': 'I'm So F--kin Bitter' Brothers Osborne & Cody Johnson Celebrate Teen Rebellion in 'Born And Raised Hell': 'It's Kind of Our Story as a Town' Eminem Takes a Trip Down Memory Lane for 'The Slim Shady Show'-Inspired Episode of Spotify's 'Billions Club'

It was both a surprise for guests, and a proper highlight, its lyrics resonating just as they did on release more than a quarter century ago.

Hayes wasn’t done there. He returned to the ARIAs stage to present Tame Impala spearhead Kevin Parker with the ARIA Global Impact Award, in recognition of his extraordinary international success and cultural impact in the past year.

For Hayes and his ex-Savage Garden bandmate Daniel Jones, the ARIA Awards is a warm and fuzzy place. At the 1997 edition, the pop group dominated with a then-record 10 wins, including album of the year and group of the year.

Savage Garden would collect a total of 14 career ARIAs, including the best-selling album award in 2000 for Affirmation, before disbanding in 2001.

The Brisbane group flew the flag high during their active years, and became one of a select handful of Australian groups to enjoy a No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Indeed, they did it twice: with 1998’s “Truly Madly Deeply,” and again in 2000 with “I Knew I Loved You,” while their 1997 track “I Want You” also entered the top 5 (peaking at No. 4). Both albums (Savage Garden at No. 3, Affirmation at No. 6) cracked the top 10 of the Billboard 200. Career album sales top 35 million units worldwide.

Earlier this year, Hayes was feted with the Excellence in Community Award at the 17th annual Music In The House charity fundraiser, in recognition both of his work with Savage Garden and his ongoing solo career, and for his community leadership and advocacy for the LGBTQIA+ community.

#726. Childish Gambino’s Politically-Charged ‘This Is America’ Joins YouTube’s Billion Views Club

"This Is America' was a politically-charged shot that rung out around the globe, a hit that touches on gun violence, racism and discrimination in America.

Childish Gambino has joined the club. YouTube’s Billion Views Club, that is, for his 2018 hit “This Is America.”

The official music video for the actor and rapper’s global smash is his first to pass the streaming milestone.

“This Is America’ was a politically-charged shot that rung out around the globe, a song that explores gun violence, racism and discrimination in the United States. It was, of course, powered by its confronting, one-take music video, directed by Hiro Murai and starring Gambino.

The recording debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart (via mcDJ/Wolf + Rothstein/RCA), bowing as the most-streamed and top-selling song of the week. It also arrived atop the U.S. Streaming Songs and Digital Song Sales charts, and topped sales and consumption charts around the globe, including Australia. Explore Childish Gambino See latest videos, charts and news

The single was the first and only Hot 100 leader for Donald Glover’s musical alter ego, who took the stage to unveil it as the musical guest on the May 5, 2018 episode of NBC’s Saturday Night Live, which he also hosted. Related Doja Cat Blasts Rockstar Games for Leaving Her Music Out of 'GTA 6': 'I'm So F--kin Bitter' Brothers Osborne & Cody Johnson Celebrate Teen Rebellion in 'Born And Raised Hell': 'It's Kind of Our Story as a Town' Eminem Takes a Trip Down Memory Lane for 'The Slim Shady Show'-Inspired Episode of Spotify's 'Billions Club'

On the red carpet of the 2018 Met Gala, Glover spoke briefly about the song and its meaning. In a comment dripping with irony, he remarked that, with “This Is America,” he simply wanted to make a song folks could play on the Fourth of July.

He elaborated in a 2023 interview for a GQ cover story, in which he said the idea for the song “started as a joke,” and that its title was “all we had” at the embryonic stage. “It started as a Drake diss, to be honest, as like a funny way of doing it. But then I was like, this s— sounds kind of hard though. So I was like, let me play with it.”

It was no joke with critics and fans. Glover and co-writer Ludwig Goransson went on to win song of the year with “America” at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards, where it became the first rap song to ever win the prestigious “Big Four” category, which recognizes songwriters. “This Is America” went on to snag a total of four Grammys, including record of the year, best music video, and snagged the MTV Video Music Award for best direction.

The song and its video have enjoyed several afterlives through covers, mashups and parodies.
