#677. Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a new type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

These unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly important in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

Now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps

In semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps

"If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving."

The key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

One of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

"Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," says Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used."

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible

The experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

"These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

What the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

This result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

The crucial factor is how quickly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A New Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the new imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

The graphene experiments have already provided an important clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

This knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open new possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover new ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

"Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light."

New catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement1, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g. oxidative addition and reductive elimination). The widespread exploitation of systems based on main-group elements therefore requires alternative elementary steps to effect turnover. Herein, we demonstrate a new catalytic platform for nucleophilic fluorination, which exploits a complex based on calcium (the fifth most Earth-abundant element) as the fluoride delivery vehicle. The key intermediate is a calcium-fluoride complex featuring a terminal Ca–F interaction, a unique structural geometry enabled by a highly sterically encumbered dianionic ligand-scaffold. This intermediate links reactants and products through F– capture and release steps, and thereby unlocks catalytic F– shuttling. Late Ca–F bond breaking in the rate-determining fluoride-delivery transition-state means that electronic and steric tuning of F– by calcium is chemically significant; proof-of-concept results show a hitherto unprecedented level of selectivity for substitution over elimination brought about by Ca-modulation. In a broader context, this work demonstrates how control over catalyst speciation and reagent binding affinity are key factors for the future development of sustainable non-transition metal paradigms in catalysis.

#675. ‘War’ Stars Sienna Miller and Dominic West Tussle Over Who Won the Divorce Drama: ‘Gwyneth Paltrow Ran So That the Rest of Us Could Walk’

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “War,” which had its season finale on Nov. 19 on HBO and HBO Max in the U.S., and drops on Nov. 20 on Sky and NOW in the U.K.

The climactic season finale of “War”—  the Sky and HBO drama series starring Sienna Miller and Dominic West as warring spouses — sees an unexpected denouement just as the couple’s increasingly bitter divorce is about to be finalized. With their lawyers still battling it out, the couple bury the hatchet and hammer out their own, more equitable deal. And with that, they walk off into the sunset.

Written and created by by George Kay (“Hijack”), the series is set to return for a second season with a new case — and new clients — to occupy the show’s fictional law firms, Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts. In Season 2, Marisa Tomei, Kelly Macdonald and David Harewood join the cast as the litigants in a high-stakes defamation case.

While Miller and West won’t reprise their roles as actress Carla Duvall and tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, neither seems quite ready to leave their characters behind. In a chat with Variety, both actors repeatedly slipped back into their roles, cheerily arguing over Morgan’s “flirting” with Carla’s barrister (Celia Imrie), Carla’s dalliance with Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) and who really won their explosive — extremely expensive — divorce battle.

Sienna Miller: It was the last thing we ever shot, so that was lovely. And I can’t really remember: A part of me probably wanted something really dramatic and cataclysmic to happen. But at the same time, I defer to the brilliance of George Kay knowing what an audience wants, because he’s written the show that people are devouring. I think the sensationalist in me wanted handbags at dawn [British idiom meaning “a dramatic showdown”], but I also in retrospect think it’s quite lovely that they had that moment. Dom?

Dominic West: “Handbags at dawn” — that would have been great. I’d have loved handbags at dawn.

Miller: I think George told us that essentially, this is what’s going to happen: The lawyers screw everything up, and [Carla and Morgan] got there in a much more simple way. So we had an idea — not at the beginning of shooting, but as we were going on — we’re like, “How does it end? What happens?!” You know, nagging like a bunch of kids. We had an inkling that that was what it was, but, again, I was 35 weeks pregnant, so the whole thing is a blur. That’s why I’m hoping Dom can jump in.

West: I remember my first thoughts were “Fucking hell, what a waste of £10 million” or whatever they spent on the lawyers when they just make it up between themselves. But actually, I think that was the point George was trying to make, and I quite like the idea that they had to go through this terrible process of lawyers and courtroom drama and going to war with each other basically in order to realize actually what they meant to each other. And how they could amicably come to an arrangement where both felt that they’d got what they deserved, and that their relationship had been quantified in a good way, in a just way.

But I think that’s the thing that really hit me was “What a fucking waste of £10 million.” But then, if you’re a billionaire, I suppose you do waste £10 million quite happily just to work out how much you like your ex-wife or ex-husband.

Miller: I do think there’s something very zeitgeist-y — and I’m not sure how he’s done this, George — but the timing of this show is so interesting. I read an article, and it was talking about “Just normalize divorce.” That the process of divorce has become so acrimonious, hellish. The children suffer. It should be something that can be amicable. Obviously, Gwyneth Paltrow ran so that the rest of us could walk. But there is a conscious uncoupling that can be lovely and better for everyone, and it left it left me feeling that it probably should be the goal to avoid conflict and remember why you love this person and how to end it in the nicest way.

West: No, we didn’t. But [Kay] didn’t tell us straight away, did he? I don’t think I knew that it was going to end so amicably.

Miller: Well, I think the audience might feel that I did because you couldn’t remember the fucking poem, could you?

West: Well, I suppose you won in that you got money for ideas and running a business that you had nothing to do with. So in that way, I suppose you were a winner.

Miller: I hope that, because [Kay] has left it amicable at the end that Dom and I can pop back.

West: What, a spinoff with Sienna and Johnny? No way!

West: I haven’t watched it all yet. I’ve only just got Sky, but I’m getting to it. I can’t wait. I watched the first episode six times, and I haven’t managed to see the rest. But I’m on it.

Miller: One of the cast texted me something very funny, which was “I hope you can come back, but Carla’s such a crazy bitch, you never know she might do something else to get in there.”

West: She’s bound to have more legal trouble.

Miller: Well, judging by your nefarious behavior in Episode 1, I think it’s coming for you too. Now it’s a hit, we really want to be invited back.

Miller: Sorry, we haven’t spoken in a while!

West: It may have ended amicably on set, but it hasn’t really ended amicably between Sienna and I in terms of the characters.

West: It was really noticeable in court: When I was talking Sienna was sitting right there, and so we’re very close to each other, we can look at each other in the eye. And it was quite thrilling to be putting the boot in, or trying to make war with someone, when you’re sitting right there. I was getting into the moment, and that was quite thrilling, to be so confrontational and to be having a go at Carla, with her being right there. The second thing was being cross-examined by Celia Imrie was quite flirty. In fact, very flirty. She was really flirty, Celia.

Miller: You say that about everyone, Dom. I think it might be you.

Miller: One thing I particularly love about when Dom answers a question about “War” is he always says “to be at war with each other.” You always drop the name, which I appreciate. I just had to say.

West: Yeah, no, good. But anyway, let me finish. So yeah, [Imrie] was quite flirty, but that was her strategy and it was in the writing. But Celia really has got such a twinkle that I loved being cross-examined by her.

Miller: Well, I have been cross-examined [in real life] a few times, I think. I’m pretty sure I have been. Archie Panjabi [who plays Morgan’s barrister] was amazing and quite stern, and I had horrible flu that day, so again, an unhelpful, blurry response. I feel like Carla felt so in-the-right in herself that I wasn’t particularly rattled. It was an intimidating environment and it was a long day, but I quite enjoyed it because I felt like I had the upper hand. Dom would disagree.

Miller: I mean, I definitely have experienced opening the door and being faced with what Carla is faced with. Not anymore, thank God. But I only read the first script when I signed on. So you’re taking a gamble. I mean, I knew she was an actress and I knew she was famous, so I assumed there might be some of that, but I didn’t really — I don’t think I want to play an actress again. Unless it’s Carla coming back in “War.”

Miller: Not particularly, no, because I didn’t know where it would all go or the spins that it would take. And no, it’s not particularly interesting for me to relive those moments or those years, but I do have an innate knowledge of them, and I suppose that’s interesting for people to see. I feel like I’m so different to Carla herself that maybe her response was an interesting thing to explore.

West: Yeah, I mean, I suppose I did have hesitations about it, but in practice, in doing it, what was quite thrilling was the thought of a billionaire getting the sort of scrutiny that the British press normally reserves for young actresses. I found that quite a thrill.

#674. A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life

To build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced new scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

To help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries

By highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the new approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," says SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically."

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. The lives of NASA's Apollo astronauts depended on it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.

First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something new.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

"This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation."

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

Other family titles include Sai Paranjpye’s “Bhago Bhoot” (2000), Rajeev Sharma’s “Bandu Boxer” (2006), Rajan Khosa’s “Gattu” (2011), Batul Mukhtiar’s “Kaphal-Wild Berries” (2013) and Pankuj Parashar’s “Banarasi Jasoos” (2015).

Chaudhary added: “What makes this edition especially exciting is the range of audiences and cinematic experiences we are looking to bring together. … Equally important for us is extending the festival experience beyond its core venues and delegates, and bringing these films to local communities across Goa so that they too can participate in and feel a part of IFFI.”

The Goa run caps a busy year for the company. PictureTime also supported the exhibition infrastructure at the Dharamshala International Film Festival and took “Pyre” to audiences in the Indian hinterland.

#671. ‘Project 11,’ Shot by 11 Directors in 11 Global Cities, Returns on Oh Short Flips (EXCLUSIVE)

“Project 11,” a 2011 survival thriller made by 11 directors working remotely from 11 cities, will be re-released Nov. 26 as the first title under Oh Short Flips‘ new Classic Shorts vertical.

The short pits 11 gamers in 11 cities against one another. Each has 11 minutes to live, and only the final survivor wins. Made years before online phenomena such as the Blue Whale Challenge caused alarm worldwide, the film dealt with fears around deadly real-world gaming dares.

Mumbai-based filmmaker Vikas Chandra drove the project, spending months finding 11 directors willing to take part. Their combined crews numbered around 100 people, spread across New York, Los Angeles, Toronto, London, Luxembourg, Tel Aviv, Dar es Salaam, Balochistan, Mumbai, Beijing and Tokyo.

The directors could not meet in person. All pre-production and storyboarding happened online. To make actors on different continents look as though they shared a frame, the filmmakers matched eyelines, faked over-the-shoulder setups and found lookalike locations in cities such as London and New York, then tied the footage together through lighting, lens choices and choreography.

The film went from script to finished cut in 149 days. A first version running 25 minutes was trimmed to 11 minutes and 11 seconds.

Alongside Chandra (Mumbai), the directors are Alessio Giorgetti (New York), Ali Ahmed Brohi (Balochistan), Dharamveer Singh Chauhan (Luxembourg), Ikematsu Hiro (Tokyo), Joseph Cohen (Tel Aviv), Nkumi Mtingwa (Dar es Salaam), Rafal Rakoczy (London), Ryan Singh (Toronto), Sydney Walsh (Los Angeles) and Yi Luo (Beijing).

“Long before the AI times, we made ‘Project 11’ with pure HumInt (Human Intelligence) – one part madness, one part ingenuity and a lot of passion, just like the write-ups called it back then,” Chandra said. “Eleven filmmakers from eleven cities who had mostly never met, connecting over late-night Skype calls, putting serious faith in strangers, and somehow scrambling crew, locations and equipment on a shoestring to pull off one crazy lab experiment in filmmaking.”

Classic Shorts will bring back well-regarded short films from earlier years that are now hard to come by, aimed at today’s online audiences.

Producer Ranjan Singh, founder of Oh Short Flips, said six months of releasing shorts on the company’s channel had shown that well-made stories always find an audience. “And we know there are so many classic shorts that are good but not available anywhere for the audience. When we did some inquiries, we realized so many filmmakers would like to release their earlier shorts for the audience to watch. Thus, we’ve decided to release these Classic Shorts also on Oh Short Flips.”

Singh added that the team made the film on a basic understanding of collaboration. “Even back then when social media wasn’t that popular we found these directors who wanted to tell a story together. Vikas led from the front and ensured the entire process was smooth and coherent. I am extremely proud that we’re starting our Classic Shorts section with ‘Project 11.'”

Chandra said that, looking back, the film was probably a little ahead of its moment. “It feels good that the film is getting another life now, on a channel dedicated to shorts.”

The news was unveiled on the sidelines of the WAVES Film Bazaar, the market arm of the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

#670. Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. New research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to new threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

Using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved."

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to new challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," says Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state."

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with new challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society."

"Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance."

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)

NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).

Jennifer Lawrence wasn’t afraid to spill tea during her appearance on the Nov. 19 episode of “Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen.”

She appeared alongside her “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” co-star Josh Hutcherson and, in her trademark honesty, fielded plenty of questions, ranging from her on-screen roles to her opinion of the “Real Housewives” franchises.

At one point, Cohen asked Lawrence to rank her on-screen kisses from best to worst, including Hutcherson (whom she smooched in “The Hunger Games: Catching Fire”), Liam Hemsworth (“The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 1”), Chris Pratt (“Passengers”), Timothée Chalamet (“Don’t Look Up”) and Bradley Cooper (“Silver Linings Playbook” and “Serena”).

Her ranking? Hutcherson was the best, and then Hemsworth, Cooper, Chalamet and Pratt at the bottom.

Elsewhere in the episode, she was candid about her breast implants. During a segment where she was discussing hot topics in the “Real Housewives” universe, Lawrence was asked about a storyline in which “Real Housewives of New York” star Hailey Glassman said her nose was broken by a woman’s breast.

“Is it a mystery to you how a boob could break Haley Glassman’s nose?” Cohen asked.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

#666. 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

New forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling new support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?"

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," said Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans."

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced."

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

The results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls showed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing important new evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

The researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

Additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal New Clues to Egypt's Dark Past

The findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve important clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" said Campbell. "Still, this study shows how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one."

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#665. Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Sikh Ruler Known as ‘Sher-e-Punjab,’ Gets Biopic, Plans 2027 Shoot (EXCLUSIVE)

Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the 19th-century Sikh ruler known as the “Sher-e-Punjab,” or Lion of Punjab, is getting a big-screen biopic, with Katha Studios and B4 Makers Studios partnering on a film that will go into production in 2027.

The two banners are pitching the project as a sweeping theatrical epic. It will trace the ruler’s life and journey, with a focus on his bravery as a leader and the mark he left on history, and is being shaped with a multigenerational audience in mind. Related Stories Martin Scorsese Says His 'Cleopatra' Movie With Angelina Jolie Was 'Ruined' by Seth Rogen and the Sony Hack: 'It Was Gonna Be Really Wild' ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Audience Award at London Film Festival

It is still early days. The film is in the initial phase of development and creative work has yet to begin. Neither company has attached a director or cast, and those details will be revealed at a later date.

“Maharaja Ranjit Singh Ji’s life and legacy offer an extraordinary canvas for cinematic storytelling. His journey, leadership and contribution to history deserve to be presented in a manner that does justice to his stature. Through this collaboration with B4 Makers Studios, we aim to create a truly grand theatrical experience that brings this remarkable chapter of history to audiences in a powerful and memorable way,” said Shibasish Sarkar, founder of Katha Studios.

Yadwinder Deep Singh, founder and designated partner of B4 Makers Studios, said the company was proud to be attached to a story of such weight and inspiration. “His legacy is deeply rooted in courage, vision and leadership. Our endeavor is to bring this extraordinary story to life through a cinematic experience that is both grand in scale and meaningful in its storytelling,” he said.

Ranjit Singh founded the Sikh Empire and ruled it from Lahore for close to four decades until his death in 1839. His story has so far played out mostly on television. Actor-politician Raj Babbar’s “Maharaja Ranjit Singh” ran on public broadcaster Doordarshan from 2010 to 2011, while Contiloe Pictures’ “Sher-e-Punjab: Maharaja Ranjit Singh,” with Damanpreet Singh in the title role, aired on Life OK in 2017.

Big-screen versions have been slower to take shape. Babbar had earlier planned a feature, “The Lord of Five Rivers: Maharaja Ranjit Singh,” that was shelved, and “Border” director J.P. Dutta lined up a Ranjit Singh biopic after his 2018 war film “Paltan.” In 2020, Guneet Monga’s Sikhya Entertainment acquired film rights to Chandigarh-based author Khushwant Singh’s novel “Maharaja in Denims,” about a teenager who believes he is the ruler reincarnated. Ranjit Singh’s son Duleep Singh, the last Sikh maharaja, was the subject of Kavi Raz’s 2017 feature “The Black Prince,” starring Satinder Sartaaj.

The project, unveiled on the sidelines of WAVES Film Bazaar, the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa, lands as large-canvas historical dramas continue to pull Indian audiences into theaters, with Laxman Utekar’s 2025 Maratha warrior saga “Chhaava” among the biggest recent hits.

#664. Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers."

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful new way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

To investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

The results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss

The new scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people."

Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang said. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be."

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

Zhang recognized that this approach could overlook important biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he said. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns."

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

The Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

They examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

The comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas showed greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance

The team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

At the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores showed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, important differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

People whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao said. "Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves."

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements showed some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he said.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially shows a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

For example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

Importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he said. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies."

Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important new direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”

#662. Climate Displacement Drama ‘The River Without a Bridge’ Heads to India’s WAVES Film Bazaar Co-Production Market

Director Praveen Morchhale is taking “The River Without a Bridge,” a family drama about a young girl uprooted by a climate disaster, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar 2026.

Told in the Assamese, Bangla, Burmese and Hindi languages, the film follows 7-year-old Aliya, who hasn’t spoken since the disaster forced her family out of Myanmar. Now living without papers in northeastern India, Aliya and her family struggle to survive and find a place to belong. As their circumstances deteriorate, she finds solace in nature. Related Stories Disney and the NFL Launch Limited-Edition Mickey & Friends Merch Ahead of Super Bowl LXI Disney Taps Adobe as 'Official AI Innovation Partner' Under Multiyear Pact

“I keep coming back to ordinary people nobody listens to. Climate change is pushing families out of their homes, and the suffering does not stop at the border. I wanted to show that through a child who can’t speak but notices everything. Aliya wants to be a tree because trees have roots and nobody asks where they’re from,” Morchhale tells Variety.

Morchhale’s previous films include “Walking With the Wind” (2017), “Widow of Silence” (2018) and “White Snow” (2025). His upcoming projects include “Floating Flowers,” about an Indian man and a 6-year-old American girl stranded at sea during the 2004 tsunami.

The film has Pranjali Morchhale of Barefoot Pictures (India) and Anja Wedell of Rokland Film (Germany) on board as producers. With $125,000 of its $495,000 budget raised, the project is seeking additional co-production partners and financing.

“Praveen writes about a painful, current subject with great care. Putting a seven-year-old at the center makes climate displacement personal. The film is beautiful to look at without turning sentimental. There’s an image at the very end of the film that has stayed with us long after reading the script,” the producers say.

Pranjali co-founded Barefoot Pictures and produced “Walking With the Wind” and “Widow of Silence.” Wedell previously worked with X-Filme Creative Pool and Czar Film before establishing Rokland Film in 2025. Her credits include “Bikini Moon,” “New Money” and “Naked Animals” (Berlinale 2020).

With the screenplay in advanced development, the team plans to shoot in 2028. “We want to meet co-producers and sales agents who believe in the film. The goal is a major festival premiere, and enough visibility to reach audiences worldwide,” say the producers.

WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.
